questions.subject: Further Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate defined operations and determine whether the result remains in the stated set.
questions.prompt: For real numbers define a ◇ b = 2a − b. Solve x ◇ (x ◇ 4) = 4, or explain why no solution exists.
questions.answer: Every real x is a solution.
questions.explanation: The inner value is 2x − 4. Substituting into the outer operation gives 2x − (2x − 4) = 4, independently of x.

markingGuide.description: Substitute and simplify the outer expression.
Conclude that every real x works.

questions.subject: Further Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate defined operations and determine whether the result remains in the stated set.
questions.prompt: A learner says the rule a ◇ b = (a + b)/2 defines a binary operation on the positive integers. Assess closure and state a larger familiar number set on which the same rule is closed.
questions.answer: The rule is not closed on the positive integers: 1 ◇ 2 = 3/2. It is closed on the positive rational numbers.
questions.explanation: An average of two positive rational numbers is positive and rational. The integer counterexample suffices to disprove closure there.

markingGuide.description: Explain that the output leaves the stated set.
Name and justify a larger closed set.

questions.subject: Further Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate defined operations and determine whether the result remains in the stated set.
questions.prompt: On the real numbers let a ★ b = a² + b. What is 2 ★ (−5)?
questions.explanation: Square the first input only and add the second. Thus 4 − 5 = −1.

questions.subject: Further Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate defined operations and determine whether the result remains in the stated set.
questions.prompt: Consider a rule that returns the larger of two inputs, or their common value if equal. On the set {2, 7, 11}, why is the rule closed?
questions.answer: Every output is one of the two inputs.
questions.explanation: The operation always selects a member of the input pair, so its output lies in the set.
options: Every output is one of the two inputs.
The set has an odd number of members.

questions.subject: Further Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Test identities, inverses, commutativity and associativity for defined operations.
questions.prompt: For real numbers define a ◇ b = a + b + ab. Show that 0 is a two-sided identity. Find all real a for which there is no b satisfying a ◇ b = 0.
questions.answer: 0 is the identity. Only a = −1 has no such b.
questions.explanation: Putting 0 on either side gives back a. The equation a + (1 + a)b = 0 gives b = −a/(1 + a) when a differs from −1. At −1 the left side is always −1.

markingGuide.description: Identify and explain the exceptional input.

questions.subject: Further Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Test identities, inverses, commutativity and associativity for defined operations.
questions.prompt: On the real numbers, define a △ b = a − b. A classmate says subtraction is associative because (a △ b) △ c and a △ (b △ c) both subtract b somewhere. Determine exactly when the expressions agree and use the result to judge the claim.
questions.answer: They agree exactly when c = 0. Subtraction is not associative.
questions.explanation: Expanding gives a − b − c and a − b + c. Equality requires −c = c, hence c = 0. Associativity requires agreement for all inputs.

markingGuide.description: Expand both expressions with the correct signs.
Explain why agreement on some triples does not establish associativity.

questions.subject: Further Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Test identities, inverses, commutativity and associativity for defined operations.
questions.prompt: For real inputs let a ★ b = a. Which statement about identity elements is true?
questions.answer: Every real number is a right identity, and there is no left identity.
questions.explanation: For any e, a ★ e = a. But e ★ a always equals e, which cannot equal every possible a.
options: Zero is the unique two-sided identity.
Every real number is a left identity, and there is no right identity.
There are no right or left identities.
Every real number is a right identity, and there is no left identity.

questions.subject: Further Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Test identities, inverses, commutativity and associativity for defined operations.
questions.prompt: For real numbers let a ⊙ b = 3a + kb, where k is fixed. Which value of k makes a ⊙ b = b ⊙ a for every pair?
questions.explanation: The difference is (3 − k)(a − b). It vanishes for all pairs only when k = 3.
